_note: Mediation analysis tested with two mediators sharing one instrument — hasMediator lists both (newline-separated), mediatorMeasure is given once since the same scale measures both.

analysis.object: Anxiety was significantly associated with muscle dysmorphia; anxiety, not depression, represents a plausible mediating route from childhood victimisation to muscle dysmorphia.
The study was retrospective and cross-sectional, which limits conclusions regarding mediation and the temporal ordering of experiences.
A larger, more representative sample would allow more stable estimation of the mediation model.

_note: sampleSizeMobilized (184, complete cases used in the main analysis) is smaller than the total recruited sampleSize (400, extracted separately in the population block) — always check for this gap rather than repeating the total.

analysis.object: Appearance- and performance-related body dissatisfaction significantly relate to eating disorder symptoms among females but not males.
Generalization is limited to healthy adult runners with low eating-disorder symptomatology; findings may not generalize to other types of athletes.
Future research should explore how body-dissatisfaction constructs vary across different athletic contexts.

_note: No 'Limitations' subsection in this article -> iadas:limites is simply omitted, never invented.

analysis.object: The drive for muscularity was found to be prevalent in Pakistani males, who are becoming victims of the current trend toward a more muscular, V-shaped body ideal.
More studies are needed on muscle dysmorphia in comparison with other variables, and the female population should also be studied.

_note: hasModerator / moderatorMeasure are ONLY filled when the article reports a formal moderation analysis (an interaction term actually tested) — a subgroup difference described narratively without a moderation model does not qualify (cf. Bravata.2003, where the discussion says 'sex appeared to moderate' but no interaction term was tested, so no moderator is extracted there).

analysis.object: Competitive anxiety predicted disordered eating symptoms more strongly among athletes with low self-esteem than among those with high self-esteem.
